extracted.intended_audience: novelists, critics, and serious readers studying the craft and form of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and composing the form of a novel: how to identify a novel’s subject, ensure unity between subject and form, manage point of view, integrate large-scale material, and craft scenes and characters so they serve the central design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the various forms of narrative consciously
rubrics_metrics.description: “They are the various forms of narrative, the forms in which a story may be told… to use them consciously and questioningly — by reading, I mean, and reading critically, the books in which they appear.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn these forms by close critical reading: follow novelists whose effects are incontestable, notice exactly how scenes and figures are presented, and study the arts and devices by which an episode is given relief or a character made intelligible and vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the novel as an art object that can be analysed
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not a piece of life, it is a piece of art like another… it should be protected by no romantic scruple.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be shy about dissecting a novel; analyse its form without feeling that you are destroying its value. The pleasure of creation is available to the reader who deliberately recreates the book by critical thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the novelist’s subject before judging form
rubrics_metrics.description: “The power that recognizes the fruitful idea and seizes it is a thing apart… we judge the novelist's eye for a subject to be his cardinal gift… till his subject is announced… the delight of treating the subject is acute and perennial.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot properly assess form until you have determined what the novelist intended to be about. Follow the writer back to the subject to understand the logic of his choices and the design that should govern the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must coincide with the subject (unity of form and matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best form is that which makes the most of its subject… the well-made book is the book in which the subject and the form coincide and are indistinguishable — the book in which the matter is all used up in the form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a novel by how completely its form expresses the subject. Disagreement between form and subject indicates superfluous or missing material and injures the story’s effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear, expressible central subject (the novel needs a centre)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A subject, one and whole and irreducible — a novel cannot begin to take shape till it has this for its support… What was the novelist's intention, in a phrase? If it cannot be put into a phrase it is no subject for a novel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel’s central idea should be compressible into a short phrase (the author suggests 'ten words'). The form of the book depends on that statement of unity; without it, the book will not cohere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain thematic unity; avoid mixing incompatible designs
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a confusion of two designs… It has no centre… two such novels… caught up together and written out… inadvertently mixed and entangled.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not couple two grand, competing themes (e.g., an intimate cycle of youth and age and a full national saga) in one work unless you have a principled way to unify them; otherwise the book will feel fragmented and centerless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure a consistent point of view and method of narration
rubrics_metrics.description: “The predominant point of view is simply his own… in one case Tolstoy is immediately beside us, narrating; in the other it is Peter and Andrew… Tolstoy is effaced.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the story will be presented through an effaced narrator, an onlooker, or the characters’ minds, and apply your choice methodically. Random or inconsistent selection of vantage points undermines unity of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusive authorial digressions and didactic pamphleteering
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is capable of thrusting into his book interminable chapters of comment and explanation, chapters in the manner of a controversial pamphlet… wherever 'the historians' are mentioned he knows that several pages can be turned at once.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from inserting sustained authorial theorising or polemic that interrupts the narrative flow. Such interruptions often prompt readers to skip and break the novel’s momentum; prefer showing through the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate large-scale or historical material so it serves the central story
rubrics_metrics.description: “The historic scene is used as a foil and a background… it very powerfully and strikingly shows what the young people are… but when treated as a separate story they do not extend or advance it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing background events (battles, national sagas, historical panorama), frame them through the characters’ experience or a consistent onlooker so they illuminate the central subject rather than become an independent, competing narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the scale of treatment to the scope of the theme
rubrics_metrics.description: “The size of the theme, and the scale upon which these scenes are drawn, imply a novel as long as our existing War and Peace; it would all be filled by Kutusov and Napoleon, if their drama were fully treated, leaving no room for another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theme requires extensive, full treatment (e.g., a national epic), devote the necessary scope to it or else refrain from attempting a second grand theme in the same work; fragmentary handling weakens both subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft scenes and figures with devices that give relief and vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The scenes and figures, as I have said, we shape, we detach… to see by what arts and devices… this episode has been given relief, that character made intelligible and vivid — we at once begin to stumble on many discoveries about the making of a novel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to the concrete techniques (selection, emphasis, detailing, placement) that make episodes striking and characters vivid. Study exemplary passages to learn how devices create relief and intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise critical vocabulary when discussing narrative structure
rubrics_metrics.description: “What is to be understood by a ‘dramatic’ narrative, a ‘pictorial’ narrative, a ‘scenic’ or a ‘generalized’ story? … they are words which have no technical acceptation in regard to a novel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loose or ambiguous terms; seek or develop clear definitions for labels applied to narrative types. A received nomenclature aids criticism and avoids confusion when diagnosing form and method.
